about: "Make it specific" prompts for Unit 2 (docs/apmacro-architecture.md, "Make it specific"): a free-response task the readers often score as too vague, a checklist, an answer that earns the point and one that misses it, and a builder (slots) that assembles the specific answer. Every number is recomputed in JUSTIFY_NUMBERS (scripts/lib/apmacro-exams.mjs).

prompts.title: GDP from spending
prompts.context:
Corlin, an invented country, billions of dollars in one year:

Consumption600
Investment150
Government purchases of goods and services200
Exports80
Imports100
Transfer payments50
prompts.prompt: Calculate Corlin's GDP, and explain why one item in the table is left out.
checklist: Gets a GDP of 930 billion dollars for the year
Leaves out transfer payments because they buy no new good or service

earns.answer: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M) = 600 + 150 + 200 + (80 - 100) = 930 billion dollars. Transfer payments (50 billion) are left out: they move income from taxpayers to recipients but pay for no new good or service.
earns.why: It writes the formula with the values, gets the total, and gives the reason for the item left out.

misses.why: Imports are subtracted, not added, and transfer payments are not purchases of output.

why.1: Imports are made abroad, so they are taken out of spending on domestic output.
Transfers buy no good or service, so they are not part of government purchases.

prompts.title: What GDP counts
prompts.prompt: This year Ada buys a used car for \$8,000 and shares in a company for \$2,000. Explain how each purchase affects this year's GDP.
checklist: Says the used car adds nothing: it was produced and counted in an earlier year
Says the shares add nothing: they are a transfer of ownership, not new output
Adds that a dealer's fee for the sale would count, as a service produced this year

earns.answer: Neither purchase adds to this year's GDP. The used car was counted in the year it was made, so selling it again is not new production. Shares in a company pass ownership of a company from one person to another; no good or service is produced. Only a fee paid this year to a dealer or broker for the sale would count, as a service produced now.
earns.why: It gives the reason for each purchase in terms of new final production and notes what would count.

misses.answer: Both add to GDP, \$10,000 in all, because Ada paid for them this year.
misses.why: Spending is counted only when it buys new final goods and services; a used car and company shares are neither.

why.1: It was counted when it was produced, so counting it again would double count.
In GDP, investment means new capital goods, not shares in a company.

prompts.title: GDP per capita and well-being
prompts.prompt: Country L's GDP grows 2% a year while its population grows 3% a year. Explain what happens to GDP per capita, and identify one thing GDP per capita still leaves out about well-being.
checklist: States GDP per capita falls, because population grows faster than GDP
Names one thing left out, such as leisure, pollution, nonmarket work or how income is shared
Links that item to why GDP per capita is an imperfect measure

earns.answer: GDP per capita is GDP divided by population. Population is growing faster than GDP, so GDP per capita falls, even though total GDP grows. It still leaves out nonmarket activity, such as care given at home, so it understates what people produce and enjoy.
earns.why: It reasons from the two growth rates to the per-person result and names a specific limitation with its effect.

misses.answer: GDP per capita rises because GDP is growing.
misses.why: Total GDP grows, but more slowly than the population, so the amount per person falls; no limitation is named.

why.1: Population grows by more than GDP, so each person's share shrinks.
why.2: The two growth rates differ, so the ratio changes.

why.1: New houses are counted, as investment.

prompts.title: Unemployment and participation rates
prompts.context:
Sennet, an invented country, millions of people:

Adult population300
Employed190
Unemployed10
prompts.prompt: Calculate Sennet's unemployment rate and its labor force participation rate, and show your work.
checklist: Finds the labor force: 190 + 10 = 200 million
Unemployment rate: 10 / 200 x 100 = 5%
Participation rate: 200 / 300 x 100, about 66.7%

earns.answer: The labor force is the employed plus the unemployed: 190 + 10 = 200 million. The unemployment rate is 10 / 200 x 100 = 5%. The participation rate is the labor force divided by the adult population: 200 / 300 x 100, about 66.7%.
earns.why: Each rate has its formula with the right denominator and the values filled in.

misses.answer: The unemployment rate is 10 / 300, about 3.3%, and participation is 190 / 300.
misses.why: The unemployment rate divides by the labor force, not the adult population, and the labor force includes the unemployed.

why.1: The unemployed are part of the labor force too.
why.2: 300 million is the adult population, which includes people not in the labor force.

why.1: That divides by adults; divide by the labor force.
why.2: That divides by the employed; divide by the labor force.

prompts.title: Natural and cyclical unemployment
prompts.prompt: Halvet's unemployment rate is 7%. Frictional unemployment is 2% and structural unemployment is 3%. Calculate the natural rate and cyclical unemployment, and explain what the cyclical rate tells you.
checklist: Natural rate = frictional + structural = 2% + 3% = 5%
Cyclical = actual - natural = 7% - 5% = 2%
Says positive cyclical unemployment means output is below potential: a downturn

earns.answer: The natural rate is frictional plus structural: 2% + 3% = 5%. Cyclical unemployment is the actual rate minus the natural rate: 7% - 5% = 2%. A positive cyclical rate means the economy is producing below its potential output, as in a contraction.
earns.why: Both formulas are written with values, and the meaning of the cyclical rate is stated.

misses.answer: The natural rate is 7%, because that is the unemployment rate.
misses.why: The natural rate leaves out cyclical unemployment; it is frictional plus structural, 5%.

why.1: 7% is the actual rate, which includes cyclical unemployment.
why.2: That adds the actual rate too; the natural rate is frictional plus structural.

why.1: That subtracts structural alone; subtract the whole natural rate.

prompts.title: Naming a type of unemployment
prompts.prompt: Pia ran a printing press for 15 years. Her plant switched to digital machines, and the jobs near her need computer skills she does not have. She is looking for work. Identify the type of unemployment and explain your answer.
checklist: Names structural unemployment
Explains her skills no longer match the jobs available
Says it is not cyclical: the cause is a change in technology, not a downturn

earns.answer: Pia is structurally unemployed. The jobs open near her need skills she lacks, because technology changed what her industry needs; her skills no longer match the jobs. It is not cyclical, since the cause is not a fall in overall spending but a change in technology.
earns.why: It names the type, ties it to the skills mismatch, and rules out the near miss.

misses.answer: Pia is cyclically unemployed, because she lost her job.
misses.why: Losing a job does not make unemployment cyclical; here the cause is a mismatch of skills after a change in technology.

why.1: Cyclical unemployment comes from a downturn in the whole economy.
why.2: Frictional unemployment is the time it takes to find a job one has the skills for.

why.label: Because
options: her skills do not match the jobs available
the economy is in a contraction

why.1: Nothing says the economy is in a downturn; her skills are the problem.

prompts.title: A price index and the inflation rate
prompts.prompt: A basket of goods cost \$250 in the base year and \$270 a year later. Calculate the CPI for the later year and the inflation rate between the two years.
checklist: Inflation rate = (108 - 100) / 100 x 100 = 8%
Notes the base year's CPI is 100

earns.answer: The CPI is the basket's cost now over its cost in the base year, times 100: 270 / 250 x 100 = 108. The base year is 100, so the inflation rate is (108 - 100) / 100 x 100 = 8%.
earns.why: The index and the rate each come with their formula and values.

misses.answer: Prices went up by \$20, so inflation is 20%.
misses.why: Inflation is the percent change in the index, (108 - 100) / 100, not the dollar change in the basket.

why.1: That divides the base-year cost by the later cost; flip it.
why.2: 20 is the change in dollars, not an index.

why.1: Divide the change by the starting value.
why.2: 108 is the index level, not its change.

prompts.title: Who loses from surprise inflation
prompts.prompt: Joss lent his sister \$1,000 for a year at a fixed 3%, expecting prices to be stable. Inflation turns out to be 6%. Explain who gains and who loses from the inflation.
checklist: Says Joss (the lender) loses: the dollars repaid buy less than he expected
Says his sister (the borrower) gains: she repays in dollars worth less
Ties the effect to the inflation being unanticipated

earns.answer: The inflation was not anticipated, so the fixed 3% did not cover it. Joss is repaid \$1,030, but prices rose 6%, so those dollars buy less than the \$1,000 he lent: the lender loses. His sister gains, because she repays in dollars that are worth less than when she borrowed.
earns.why: It names both sides, explains with buying power, and ties it to the inflation being unexpected.

misses.answer: Everyone loses from inflation because prices are higher.
misses.why: Unanticipated inflation moves buying power from lenders to borrowers; the borrower here gains.

why.1: The dollars he gets back buy less than he expected.
She repays in dollars worth less, which helps her.

prompts.title: Real GDP from the deflator
prompts.prompt: Riven's nominal GDP is 1,320 billion dollars and its GDP deflator is 110. Calculate real GDP, and explain what the deflator says about prices compared with the base year.
checklist: Real GDP = nominal / deflator x 100 = 1,320 / 110 x 100
Gets 1,200 billion dollars
Says prices are 10% higher than in the base year

earns.answer: Real GDP = nominal GDP / deflator x 100 = 1,320 / 110 x 100 = 1,200 billion dollars. A deflator of 110 means prices are on average 10% higher than in the base year, so real GDP is smaller than nominal GDP.
earns.why: It divides by the deflator (not multiplies), shows the values, and reads the deflator correctly.

misses.answer: Real GDP is 1,320 x 1.1 = 1,452 billion dollars.
misses.why: That multiplies by the deflator; removing price increases means dividing by it.

op.label: To remove price changes
options: divide by the deflator and multiply by 100

why.1: Multiplying adds the price rise again; divide to take it out.
That multiplies by 1.1.

prompts.title: An output gap
prompts.prompt: Bracken's potential output is 900 billion dollars, and its real GDP this year is 860 billion dollars. Identify the output gap and explain what it implies for unemployment.
checklist: Finds real GDP is 40 billion dollars below potential output
Calls it a negative output gap
Says unemployment is above the natural rate: cyclical unemployment is positive

earns.answer: Real GDP is 860, which is 900 - 860 = 40 billion dollars below potential output: a negative output gap. The economy is not using all its resources, so unemployment is above the natural rate and cyclical unemployment is positive.
earns.why: It sizes the gap, names its sign, and links it to unemployment.

misses.answer: The economy is 860 billion dollars, so it is in a boom.
misses.why: Real GDP below potential means a negative gap and high unemployment, not a boom.

why.1: Real GDP is below potential, so the gap is negative.
Output below potential means idle workers, so unemployment is above the natural rate.
